drugs.name: Bedaquiline
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase, killing both replicating and nonreplicating bacilli; CYP-metabolized (drug interactions); long half-life
drugs.adverseEffects: Boxed warning for QT prolongation, so avoid in long QT; hepatotoxicity from the oxidative stress of its M2 metabolite

drugs.name: Pretomanid
drugs.mechanism: Nitroimidazole prodrug activated by the mycobacterial Ddn nitroreductase; releases nitric oxide and reactive nitrogen species that break down the mycolic acid wall; long half-life
drugs.adverseEffects: Peripheral neuropathy, QT prolongation and hepatotoxicity; baseline and regular ECGs and periodic liver tests through the roughly 6-month course
drugs.use: Pulmonary XDR-TB, or MDR-TB that is treatment-intolerant or nonresponsive, given with bedaquiline and linezolid for about 6 months

drugs.name: Azithromycin
drugs.mechanism: Macrolide: binds 50S and blocks translocation; bacteriostatic. Long half-life allows a once-daily 5-day course; no CYP inhibition. Resistance: efflux, 23S rRNA methylation
drugs.use: MAC in advanced HIV (CD4 < 50) with ethambutol; Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila and Legionella pneumonia; pertussis; chlamydia cover beside IM ceftriaxone for gonorrhea; safe in pregnancy and children

drugs.name: Clarithromycin
drugs.mechanism: Macrolide 50S translocation blocker dosed twice daily; inhibits CYP enzymes, so interactions; better absorbed and fewer GI effects than the oldest macrolide
drugs.use: Alternative macrolide partner to ethambutol for MAC; more active against streptococci, staphylococci, H. pylori, Moraxella, Legionella and M. pneumoniae

drugs.name: Erythromycin
drugs.mechanism: The oldest macrolide: 50S translocation block, but needs several doses a day, causes more GI upset and inhibits CYP3A4
drugs.use: Alternative to penicillin for streptococcal pharyngitis in a penicillin-allergic patient
